extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, historians, and policymakers interested in democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Tocqueville's evaluative criteria for judging democratic vs. aristocratic institutions, civic habits, and law in 19th-century societies (especially the United States). Useful for readers comparing forms of government or deriving normative lessons about democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality and temporary alliances
rubrics_metrics.description: “Taking care always to keep ourselves, by suitable establishments, in a respectable defensive posture, we may safely trust to temporary alliances for extraordinary emergencies.” (Washington’s maxim as cited)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville uses Washington's advice as a standard for prudent foreign policy: maintain a respectable defense, avoid entangling permanent alliances, and rely on temporary alliances only for extraordinary emergencies. The United States' foreign policy is praised for abstaining from European affairs and for having 'no foreign interests to discuss' due to geography and chosen policy; foreign policy thus consists more in abstaining from interference than in active exertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid habitual hatred or fondness in foreign relations
rubrics_metrics.description: “The nation which indulges towards another an habitual hatred or an habitual fondness is in some degree a slave. It is a slave to its animosity or to its affection...,” (Washington’s remark as cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative norm, Tocqueville highlights that habitual emotional attachments (hatred or fondness) compromise a nation's independence of judgment and lead it to act against its duty and interest. Foreign policy should be guided by interest and prudence, not by persistent passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid soliciting reciprocal privileges from foreign powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Jefferson's maxim: “the Americans ought never to solicit any privileges from foreign nations, in order not to be obliged to grant similar privileges themselves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a policy principle, soliciting special privileges creates obligations to reciprocate and can entangle a state; Tocqueville presents this as a constraint that simplifies U.S. foreign policy and preserves independence of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracies are ill-suited for foreign affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: “Foreign politics demand scarcely any of those qualities which a democracy possesses; and they require, on the contrary, the perfect use of almost all those faculties in which it is deficient.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville asserts a general criterion: effective foreign policy requires perseverance, secrecy, sustained execution of complex undertakings, and patient calculation—qualities democracies typically lack (because of passion, short attention spans, lack of secrecy). Thus democracies are often inferior to aristocracies in conducting international strategy and achieving large, long-term designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy's fixity of purpose and aptitude for large designs
rubrics_metrics.description: “Almost all the nations which have ever exercised a powerful influence... have been governed by aristocratic institutions... nothing in the world has so absolute a fixity of purpose as an aristocracy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville uses aristocracy as the standard for durable national projects: an aristocracy combines sustained energy, continuity, and collective self-control that enable the conception and execution of vast, long-term state undertakings—advantages democracies lack in foreign policy and in crafting convergent legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation should tend to promote the welfare of the greatest number
rubrics_metrics.description: “Democratic laws generally tend to promote the welfare of the greatest possible number; for they emanate from the majority of the citizens...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a normative criterion for laws, Tocqueville holds that the democratic aim—favoring the majority's interests—is a principal advantage of democratic legislation. Even if democratic laws are imperfectly drawn, their purpose (serving the greatest number) is judged positively relative to aristocratic legislation that concentrates wealth and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracies are more expert legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: “Aristocracies are infinitely more expert in the science of legislation than democracies ever can be... They form lasting designs which they mature with the assistance of favorable opportunities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an evaluative standard: aristocratic legislatures are better at drafting coherent, skillful, long-term legal frameworks because they have self-control, expertise, and the capacity to make laws converge toward a single purpose; democratic laws are often ineffective or inopportune despite better aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic adaptability: capacity to commit faults and repair them
rubrics_metrics.description: “The great advantage of the Americans consists in their being able to commit faults which they may afterward repair.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville treats flexibility and changeability as an advantage: democracies can survive transient bad laws because they can more readily alter them. This criterion depends on a community's capacity to endure transitory errors without destruction and to later correct them through political processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of public officers' interests with the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the American democracy public officers have no permanent interests distinct from those of the majority.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a measure of institutional health, Tocqueville values that public officials in democracies lack a separate caste-interest; their interests are identified with the majority’s, which reduces the risk of sustained policies harming the public interest. Even if individuals lack talent or virtue, the identification of interests helps check systematic abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorter tenure limits entrenched corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic magistrates are more apt to misuse power but “they possess it for a shorter period of time.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because democratic officials hold office for limited terms, corruption and incapacity are less likely to become durable, organized interests. Maladministration is treated as an isolated, temporary occurrence rather than a permanent collective harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocratic cohesion creates durable class interests
rubrics_metrics.description: “The common purpose which connects the interest of the magistrates in aristocracies with that of a portion of their contemporaries identifies it with that of future generations... it induces them to coalesce, and to combine their efforts in order to attain an end which does not always ensure the greatest happiness of the greatest number.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville evaluates aristocratic rule as prone to creating long-lasting, intergenerational class-driven policy that can systematically favor a minority; this cohesion can produce large-scale effects (good or bad) over time because it ties present power to future interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of patriotism: instinctive vs. reflective
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an “instinctive, disinterested... feeling” of patriotism and another “more rational... coeval with the spread of knowledge... nurtured by the laws... confounded with the personal interest of the citizen.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a civic standard, Tocqueville distinguishes quick, passionate (instinctive) patriotism—which can produce heroic effort but is ephemeral—from reflective patriotism grounded in rights and law—which is steadier and more productive of continuous civic engagement. Societies should aim to cultivate reflective patriotism when instinctive patriotism wanes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political participation breeds civic interest
rubrics_metrics.description: “The most powerful, and perhaps the only, means of interesting men in the welfare of their country which we still possess is to make them partakers in the Government.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville treats the exercise of political rights as the primary practical method for connecting private interest to public interest: granting and extending political participation promotes civic zeal, knowledge of rights, and an active concern for the common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notion of rights formed by possession/exercise of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy of the child and toys: as a child learns possession and fears losing it, he learns to respect rights; likewise property ownership and exercise of political rights instill recognition of rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a pedagogical standard: rights are best inculcated empirically by giving people something to lose or to exercise (property, political franchise). It explains why property distribution and broad participation create a culture that respects rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular origin and personal stake increase respect for the law
rubrics_metrics.description: “This popular origin, which impairs the excellence and the wisdom of legislation, contributes prodigiously to increase its power... everyone is personally interested in enforcing the obedience of the whole community to the law... he regards it as a contract to which he is himself a party.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville proposes that laws deriving from popular authority and in which individuals see their own stake command stronger obedience and legitimacy. Even imperfect laws gain compliance because citizens feel authorship and personal interest in their enforcement; exceptions include those whose class position makes them wary (e.g., the wealthy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy protects majority interests, not necessarily all classes
rubrics_metrics.description: “The advantage of democracy does not consist... in favoring the prosperity of all, but simply in contributing to the well-being of the greatest possible number.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative caveat, Tocqueville insists democracy's central normative claim is maximizing welfare for the largest number; this implies trade-offs (some classes, especially the wealthy, may be disadvantaged or anxious), and democratic law must be assessed on that basis rather than on universal parity.
